## Introduction

A subdural hematoma develops from the accumulation of blood in the plane between the dura mater and the arachnoid membrane (see Image. Subdural Hematoma Tentorium). An accurate understanding of subdural hematoma depends on knowledge of the neuroanatomical coverings of the brain. The brain is composed of interconnected neurons and supporting connective tissue that are highly susceptible to injury without adequate protection. Protection begins with the scalp and bony skull and continues internally with the meninges, which consist of 3 distinct layers.

Along the inner surface of the skull, the dura mater forms a dense layer and adheres to the periosteum through its outer surface, while facing the arachnoid mater through its inner surface. The arachnoid mater lies beneath the dura as the middle meningeal layer. The innermost meningeal layer is the pia mater. Bridging veins cross the plane between the dura and the arachnoid to drain blood coming from the brain into the dural venous system. Rupture of these thin-walled bridging veins under opposing mechanical forces releases blood into the subdural space, resulting in a subdural hematoma.

A larger potential space between the dura mater and the brain, commonly observed in the developing or aging brain due to cerebral volume loss, allows cerebrospinal fluid to occupy a greater volume within the spaces between the bridging veins. This expansion stretches the veins and increases vulnerability to rupture. Small extravasations may resolve spontaneously, whereas larger hemorrhages expand the subdural space, promote progressive blood layering around the brain, create mass effect, and ultimately precipitate herniation of cerebral structures.

The term subdural hematoma covers biologically distinct entities that share a location but not a mechanism. Acute subdural hematoma usually follows trauma and behaves as an expanding extra-axial mass coupled to primary parenchymal injury. Chronic subdural hematoma is an inflammatory neomembrane disease sustained by angiogenesis, hyperfibrinolysis, and recurrent microhemorrhage. This distinction matters because acute lesions are managed with an emphasis on the risk of imminent herniation, whereas chronic lesions are managed with a focus on symptom progression, recurrence, and frailty-sensitive recovery.

The usual temporal framework remains clinically useful. An acute subdural hematoma is blood imaged within the first 72 hours after injury. Subacute lesions usually occupy a 3- to 21-day interval. Chronic lesions are typically defined after 3 weeks, although mixed-density and acute-on-chronic collections show that radiographic appearance reflects repeated bleeding episodes. A small acute clot can therefore evolve into a chronic, membrane-lined collection, while a chronic hematoma can acquire hyperdense acute components after interval rebleeding.

The disease burden is rising. Population aging, cerebral atrophy, higher fall frequency, and widespread antithrombotic exposure have expanded the pool of patients at risk for both traumatic acute lesions and nonacute recurrent collections. Contemporary United States data estimate chronic subdural hematoma incidence at 17.3 per 100,000 persons per year, with incidence exceeding 350 per 100,000 in men aged 85 years or older. Chronic subdural hematoma is projected to become the most common cranial neurosurgical disease by 2030 if current demographic trends persist. In parallel, older adults now represent a large share of acute subdural hematoma presentations and often arrive with baseline frailty, anticoagulant use, or both, which alters operative risk, postoperative recovery, and long-term mortality.

## Etiology

Trauma remains the dominant cause of acute subdural hematoma. Rapid acceleration-deceleration can shear bridging veins, disrupt cortical arteries, or convert a parenchymal contusion into a subdural collection. In younger patients, this often follows high-energy mechanisms, eg, motor vehicle collisions or major falls. In older adults, the same lesion may result from a seemingly minor ground-level fall because cerebral atrophy stretches bridging veins and enlarges the subdural compartment, thereby increasing vessel vulnerability even with low impact energy. Alcohol use disorder, seizure-related falls, thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy, and oral anticoagulants amplify both the likelihood of hemorrhage and the probability of interval expansion.

Chronic subdural hematoma usually follows minor trauma, but the absence of remembered trauma is common and should not lower diagnostic suspicion. Underlying etiologies have 2 especially important pathways. The first is evolution from a traumatic subdural hygroma, a cerebrospinal fluid-rich collection formed after separation of the dura-arachnoid interface. The second is the transformation of a small acute subdural hematoma into a membrane-lined chronic cavity. Both pathways require persistence of a potential space and impaired brain re-expansion, which is why advanced age and cerebral atrophy are such consistent risk factors. Chronic subdural hematoma is also more common in patients with a higher degree of baseline frailty, functional impairment, and comorbid conditions.

Atraumatic acute subdural hematoma deserves an expanded etiologic search. Ruptured aneurysm, cortical arteriovenous malformation, cortical arterial rupture, tumors, coagulopathy, and cerebral venous thrombosis can all present with a subdural pattern of hemorrhage. These causes are uncommon, but they become more plausible when the hemorrhage is interhemispheric or basal, when subarachnoid blood accompanies the subdural clot, when headache is thunderclap in onset, or when the clinical history does not support trauma. Failure to recognize these entities can misclassify a treatable vascular lesion as simple trauma and delay definitive therapy.

Etiology also influences recurrence. Chronic collections with active rebleeding biology, mixed or hyperdense components, extensive membranes, or ongoing antithrombotic exposure recur more often after standard evacuation because the disease substrate persists after decompression. This observation explains why evacuation alone is highly effective for mass relief but incompletely addresses the membrane biology that drives chronic disease, an insight that now underpins interest in embolization and pharmacologic strategies.

Pediatric Etiologies

In pediatric patients, trauma represents the most common cause of subdural hematoma, with blunt and shearing forces serving as major contributing mechanisms. Use of cranium extraction devices and traumatic birth delivery accounts for a majority of subdural hematomas during the newborn period. Beyond the newborn stage and up to age 2 years, subdural hematoma most often results from accidental injury or intentional head trauma.

Subdural hematoma caused by intentional injury commonly receives the designation “shaken baby syndrome.” This term reflects the repetitive back-and-forth motion of the brain within the skull, during which fragile bridging veins are subject to rupture due to violent acceleration and deceleration forces acting against cerebral inertia (see Image. Shaken Baby Syndrome). Infants remain particularly vulnerable because insufficient neck muscle strength limits their ability to stabilize their heads during such events. Retinal hemorrhage frequently accompanies this mechanism and serves as a pathognomonic finding associated with shaken baby syndrome.

## Pathophysiology

Acute subdural hematoma injures through mass effect and through association with underlying brain trauma. A rapidly expanding extra-axial clot elevates intracranial pressure, distorts the falx and tentorium, compresses cortical and deep venous drainage, and reduces cerebral perfusion pressure. The clot itself is therefore only a part of the lesion. Many patients also harbor contusions, traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage, or diffuse axonal injury, which explains why the outcome is often poorer than clot volume alone would suggest. When basal cisterns efface, and pupils become asymmetric, the physiology has usually shifted from compensable intracranial hypertension to transtentorial herniation. This transition mandates immediate action, as delay can convert a potentially reversible mass lesion into secondary ischemic injury.

Chronic subdural hematoma follows a different biologic course. The initiating event is best understood as injury and separation of the dural border cell layer, a specialized interface between dura and arachnoid. This insult may follow trivial trauma, hygroma formation, or a small acute bleed. Border cell disruption triggers fibroproliferation and the development of outer and inner membranes that enclose a new pathologic cavity. The outer membrane becomes the principal engine of disease because it is vascular, inflamed, and biologically unstable.

Enlargement is driven by 3 interlocking processes. The first is angiogenesis. The outer membrane produces fragile neocapillaries with poor endothelial integrity. The second is hyperfibrinolysis, which prevents stable clot organization and favors recurrent low-volume bleeding into the cavity. The third is inflammation, which promotes further membrane growth and increases vascular permeability. Together they create a self-reinforcing cycle of exudation, microhemorrhage, membrane formation, and repeated reactivation.

This biology explains the characteristic imaging heterogeneity of chronic disease. Mixed density on computed tomography often reflects blood products of different ages within a single cavity, rather than simple partial liquefaction. Laminar and separated patterns signal active rebleeding phases, whereas trabecular architecture is more often seen in later absorption stages. The same framework explains recurrence. Surgical drainage removes mass and symptoms, but unless the membrane biology quiets and the brain reexpands, the residual cavity remains available for renewed exudation and bleeding. Hyperdense components, extensive membranes, bilateral disease, and poor postoperative reexpansion, therefore, correlate with recurrence risk.

The middle meningeal artery sits at the center of modern translational interest because it supplies the vascularized outer membrane. Embolization targets this arterial inflow to devascularize the membrane, thereby reducing exudation and rebleeding at the source. Chronic subdural hematoma can be considered a membrane-driven, inflammatory vascular lesion containing blood. That mechanistic reframing is one of the most important conceptual advances in the field.

Pediatric Pathophysiology

In shaken baby syndrome or battered infant syndrome, violent shaking of the head generates rapid acceleration and deceleration forces that cause the brain to move in a direction opposite to the meninges, leading to rupture of the bridging veins and bleeding into the subdural space. This potential space can accumulate a substantial volume of blood at various stages, presenting as acute or subacute forms. Initial hemorrhage frequently remains unrecognized and later becomes evident as a chronic subdural hematoma.

With sufficient blood accumulation occupying a large portion of the intracranial compartment, the cerebral midline shifts toward the contralateral side. This shift compresses brain structures against the inner surface of the calvarium, thereby reducing the volume of the lateral, third, and fourth ventricles. Progressive limitation of intracranial space allows volumetric forces to displace the uncal portion of the temporal lobe toward the foramen magnum, resulting in cerebral herniation (see Image. Subdural Hematoma and Uncal Herniation).

## History and Physical

The bedside history should first determine whether the presentation fits an acute mass-effect emergency or a nonacute collection. In acute subdural hematoma, the key questions are mechanism, time from injury, loss of consciousness, seizure, persistent vomiting, intoxicants, antithrombotic exposure, and interval decline after the trauma. Older adult patients on anticoagulants may present after a low-energy fall with symptoms disproportionate to the reported impact, and that mismatch should heighten concern, not reassure the clinician.

Acute symptoms cluster around raised intracranial pressure and focal compression. Headache, nausea, vomiting, somnolence, aphasia, hemiparesis, gaze deviation, and progressive decline in Glasgow Coma Scale score are typical. Pupillary asymmetry, extensor posturing, or a new respiratory pattern change usually indicates herniation physiology and identifies a time-critical pathway to surgical decompression. Seizure may occur at presentation or during early progression, especially when cortical contusions coexist.

In chronic subdural hematoma, a gait decline is common and often more informative than headache in older adults. Patients may report repeated falls, slowed cognition, apathy, fluctuating confusion, new urinary urgency, mild aphasia, hand clumsiness, hemiparesis, or facial droop. Because these symptoms evolve over days to weeks, chronic subdural hematoma routinely mimics ischemic stroke, dementia, delirium, medication toxicity, or normal-pressure hydrocephalus. Bilateral collections are particularly deceptive because lateralizing findings may be muted, and the dominant presentation may be global cognitive or functional decline.

The examination must capture the variables that change management immediately. Glasgow Coma Scale score, pupillary size and reactivity, presence of focal motor deficit, aphasia, neglect, seizure activity, and brainstem signs should be documented before sedation or intubation whenever possible. In nonacute disease, gait and baseline function provide critical context, clarifying the source of symptoms and helping define postoperative goals. The assessment should also establish premorbid independence and frailty. Contemporary population data show that many chronic subdural hematoma patients are functionally impaired before the hemorrhage, and frailty is strongly associated with later mortality. This means that 2 patients with identical scans can merit different recommendations because the likelihood of returning to baseline differs substantially.

Certain bedside constellations should trigger immediate escalation. A declining Glasgow Coma Scale score, new anisocoria, worsening hemiparesis, recurrent emesis, or refractory severe headache in any patient with known or suspected subdural hematoma should be treated as evidence of progression until imaging proves otherwise. In a stable patient with subtle gait or cognitive change after a fall, a low threshold for imaging should be maintained, because chronic subdural hematoma is common, treatable, and frequently overlooked when the presentation is framed as simple deconditioning or confusion.

Clinical Features in Pediatric Patients

History-taking and physical examination in infants and children can present significant challenges, particularly in cases of suspected abusive head trauma. Clinicians may encounter injuries that conflict with the caretaker’s account, and any suspicion should prompt a thorough clinical evaluation and notification of the appropriate child protection authorities. Newborns who experience traumatic birth often present with a history of difficult passage through the birth canal. Particular attention must be paid to the use of forceps or vacuum extraction devices during delivery, as these interventions can contribute to intracranial injury.

Caretakers and family members frequently report abnormal breathing patterns, apneic episodes, behavioral changes, vomiting, abnormal movements, or seizures in patients with subdural hematomas. Careful observation may reveal subtle or overt alterations in mental status, ranging from irritability to lethargy. When trauma history is apparent, external scalp injuries or palpable cephalohematomas may be present. In infants with an open fontanel, palpation may demonstrate a tense, noncompliant, or bulging fontanel. Other signs of abusive trauma may appear on the skin as bruising or limb deformities. Occasionally, physical examination may reveal no visible external injury, emphasizing the importance of careful assessment and vigilance.
